title: Fancy French Endings
kidRule: Some words from French keep their French endings: Q-U-E says /k/, E-T often says 'ay', and E-A-U says 'oh'!
hint: This word came from French, and its ending is spelled the French way, not the way it sounds. Can you picture the French ending?
reminder: French endings: the /k/ sound is spelled Q-U-E, 'ay' is spelled E-T, and 'oh' is spelled E-A-U.

check.question: Why does BALLET end with the letters E-T when we hear 'ay'?
check.correctAnswer: It came from French, and the French ending ET often says 'ay'!
distractors: Because the T was added by mistake long ago
Because every word that ends in ET says 'ay'

words.def: A kind of dancing that tells a story with graceful jumps and twirls.
words.sent: My sister wears pink slippers to her ballet class.
words.story: The word is French, and dancers all over the world still use French names for their steps, like 'pirouette' for a spin!
words.card: The *ballet* dancer twirled on top of a giant beach *ball*!

words.def: Something very old that people still treasure, like a hundred-year-old clock.
words.sent: That wooden rocking horse is an antique from long ago.
words.story: Many people say a thing must be at least 100 years old before you can call it an antique!
words.card: The *ant* rode an *antique* tricycle to the picnic!

words.def: A meal where the food is set out on a long table and you help yourself.
words.sent: We filled our plates at the breakfast buffet.
words.story: In France, this was first the name of the piece of furniture that the food was set out on!
words.card: The *buff* gorilla lifted the *buffet* table to look for bananas!

words.def: The only one of its kind; not like any other.
words.sent: Every snowflake has a unique shape.
words.story: Your fingerprints are unique. Nobody else in the world has the same ones, not even a twin!
words.card: My *uni*corn is *unique* because it only eats purple noodles!

words.def: A bunch of flowers picked and tied together.
words.sent: I picked a bouquet of daisies for my teacher.
words.story: Long ago in French, this word meant 'a little wood', which is a small clump of trees!
words.card: I picked a *bouquet* of stinky socks just for y*ou*!

words.def: A big, high piece of land that is flat on top.
words.sent: The hikers rested on a wide plateau above the valley.
words.story: This word comes from French, where 'plat' means flat. One plateau in Asia is so high that people call it the Roof of the World!
words.card: On the windy *plateau*, a goat balanced a *plate* of cupcakes!

words.def: A cold, sweet treat made from frozen fruit juice.
words.sent: I chose a scoop of raspberry sorbet for dessert.
words.story: This treat's name came into English from French. It usually has no milk or cream at all, just fruit, sugar, and ice!
words.card: I *bet* you can't eat lemon *sorbet* without making a funny face!

words.sent: The painter wore a red beret tipped to one side.
words.story: This is a French word. Shepherds in the mountains between France and Spain wore these wool hats to stay warm!
words.card: 'Come h*ere*!' I called, but my *beret* rolled away like a pancake!

words.def: A small shop that sells special things like clothes or gifts.
words.sent: Mom bought a scarf at a little boutique downtown.
words.story: In French, this is simply the everyday word for a shop!
words.card: The poodle ran *out* of the *boutique* wearing six sparkly hats!

words.def: A chest of drawers for keeping clothes in. It can also mean an office.
words.sent: I keep my socks in the top drawer of my bureau.
words.story: In French, this word means a desk. Long ago it was the name of the cloth that covered a writing desk!
words.card: The *bur*ping frog hid in the top drawer of my *bureau*!
